title: Roused in Old Age, and the Plain Sense
english: Then, too, though we old men were already numbed by time, by the weakness of the body, and by the multitude of our afflictions (for the many that have stirred around us have weighed down our life), you have nevertheless roused us; and, fervent in spirit (Romans 12:11), you are bringing us, who had grown cold, back to a measure of wakefulness and lively activity, like animals that winter in their dens.
The saying, then, can be understood simply, as it stands, and it can also admit a more varied explanation.
The simpler sense, the one that can present itself readily to anyone, is this: that Cain must pay a sevenfold penalty for his sins (Genesis 4:15).

For it is not the part of a just judge to fix equal requitals for equal deeds; rather, the one who began the evil must repay what he owes with something added, if he himself is to be made better by the punishments and to make the rest more self-controlled by his example.
translator_notes: The sentence runs on from the previous section: Ἔπειτα καί ('then, too') answers τέως μέν ('first of all').
νεναρκηκότας (perfect active participle of ναρκάω): 'numbed'. ὡς τὰ φωλεύοντα τῶν ζώων: 'like animals that winter in their dens'.
ζέων τῷ πνεύματι ('fervent in spirit') quotes Romans 12:11.

Two copy-text readings are taken by sense. ἀποίκιλον: the next sentence's 'the simpler sense' needs a second, more complex reading, so it is read as καὶ ποικίλον ('a more varied explanation'); the standard English of Basil's Letter 260 takes it the same way. ἢ μέλλει: 'or he will become better' makes no sense here, so it is read as a condition ('if he is to be made better').
The section ends mid-sentence ('So then, since…'); the clause continues in the next section.

title: The First Sense and a Deeper Question
english: …it has been ordained that Cain should pay the penalty for his sins seven times over, the one who kills him, it says, will release him from what divine judgment decreed against him (Genesis 4:15). This is the sense that presents itself here on a first reading.

But since the mind of the more diligent naturally searches the depths, it looks for the justice of it: how are the punishments fulfilled in the “seven times”? Are the sins seven? Or is the sin one, and the punishments for that one sin seven?

Now Scripture always limits the number for the forgiveness of sins to seven. “How often,” he says, “will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him?” (it is Peter speaking to the Lord) “Up to seven times?” (Matthew 18:21). Then comes the Lord’s answer: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matthew 18:22). For the Lord did not move on to another number, but…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, continuing 'So then, since…' (Οὐκοῦν ἐπειδή) from the end of the previous section, and breaks off mid-sentence (ἀλλὰ τὸν); the next section resumes with 'multiplied the seven'. Ellipses mark both breaks.

παραλύσει … τούτῳ τῷ ὑπὸ τῆς θείας κρίσεως ἐπ' αὐτῷ δεδογμένον: the copy-text has the dative τούτῳ τῷ where an accusative object would be expected; rendered by sense, 'release him from what divine judgment decreed against him'.
πότερον sets up an either/or, but the copy-text has no ἤ before the second option; 'Or' is supplied in English to mark the alternative.
πῶς ἐν τῷ ἑπτάκις πληροῦται καὶ τὰ ἐκδικούμενα is one question, with τὰ ἐκδικούμενα ('the punishments') as its subject.
Matthew 18:22 is rendered 'seventy times seven' because the letter's argument is that the Lord multiplied seven rather than changing the number.

title: The Number Seven in the Law and This Age
english: …multiplied the seven and set the limit within it. And after seven years the Hebrew was set free from slavery (Exodus 21:2). Seven weeks of years made up the renowned Jubilee for the people of old (Leviticus 25:8–10), in which the land kept sabbath, debts were cancelled, and there was release from slavery; and in the number seven a new life, as it were, began afresh, with the old in a way reaching its completion.

These things are types of this present age, which circles round through the seven days and runs past us. In it the penalties for lesser sins are paid off, in keeping with the loving care of the good Master, so that we may not be handed over to punishment in the endless age. The “seven times,” then, is used because of its kinship with this world, as with world-loving people, from them…
translator_notes: Continues the sentence from the previous section: the Lord did not move to another number, but multiplied the seven.
δι' ἑπτὰ ἐτῶν: 'after seven years' (Exodus 21:2). The Jubilee of seven weeks of years is Leviticus 25:8-10.
ἐκτίσεις: penalties paid off. Lesser sins are paid for in this age, so that we escape endless punishment.
φιλοκόσμων: 'world-loving'. The copy-text breaks off mid-sentence; the English follows it up to the break.
baehrens: PG 77; CPG 5379? / Ep. 80 Ad Optimum (Cain) ep rem close
